passages.original: alterum vero, ut ad scientiam prius veniat quod post gravitas moralis exerceat, quibus inquirendis permulta esse necesse est, quae vestigantem animum a recti itinere non minimumprogressionededucant:utin multisevenit Epicuro, qui atomis mundum constare putat, et honestum corporis voluptate metitur. Hæc autem idcircohuicatquealiisaccidisse manifestum est, quoniam perimperitiam disputandi quidquid ratiocinatione comprehenderant hæc in res quoque ipsas evenire arbitrantur.
passages.english: The other is that what moral seriousness will afterwards put into practice should first come to knowledge. In investigating these things there must be a great many [points] that lead the searching mind away from the right path by no small advance, as happens in many cases with Epicurus, who thinks that the world consists of atoms and measures the honourable by bodily pleasure. It is clear that this befell him and others because, through inexperience in disputation, they suppose that whatever they had grasped by reasoning also happens in the things themselves.
passages.notes: Many words run together in the scan; read as 'non minimum progressione deducant', 'idcirco huic atque aliis'. 'Inquisitionis certa' in the preceding context appears corrupt. The sense of 'non minimum progressione' is uncertain.

passages.original: Ignorata differentiaspecies quoque necesse estignorari.Quomodo ergo fieri potest ut quamlibet differentiam possimus agnoscere,si omnino quæ sit nominis hujus significatio nesciamus ? Jam vero proprii tantus usus est, ut Aristoteles quoque singulorum prædicamentorum propria perquisierit, quas propria esse quis deprehenderitantequam quid omninositpropriumdiscat* Nec in his tantum proprii haec cognitio valet quae singulis nominibus efferuntur,ut hominis risibile, verum etiam in his quae in locum diffinitionis adhibentur.Omnia enim propria rem subjectam quodam termino descriptionis includunt,quod suo loco quoque opportunius commemorabo.Accidentis quoque cognitio quantum afferat,quis dubitare queat,cum videat inter decem praedicamenta novem tenere accidentis naturas ?Quae quomodo accidentis esse putabimus,si omnino quid sit accidens ignoremus?
passages.english: If difference is unknown, species too must be unknown. How then can it come about that we recognise any difference whatever, if we do not know at all what the meaning of this name is? Again, the use of property is so great that Aristotle too searched out the properties of the individual categories. Who could detect that these are properties before learning what a property is at all? Nor is this knowledge of property useful only in those things that are expressed by single names, such as 'capable of laughter' of man, but also in those that are used in place of a definition. For all properties enclose the subject thing within a certain boundary of description, which I shall also mention more fittingly in its place. And who could doubt how much the knowledge of accident contributes, when he sees that among the ten categories nine hold the nature of accidents? How shall we think these belong to accident if we are wholly ignorant of what an accident is?
passages.notes: 'quas propria esse' read as 'quae'. The question mark is restored for the printed asterisk after 'discat'.

passages.original: Cum sit necessarium, Chrysaori, et ad eam quæ est apud Aristotelem praedicamentorum doctrinam nosse quid sit genu.s,quid differentia, quid species, quid proprium, et quid accidens,el ad diffinitionum assignationem,et omnino ad ea quæ in divisione et in demonstratione sunt, utili itarum rerum speculatione compendiosam tibi tradilionem faciens, tentabo breviter, velut introductionis modo, ea quæ ab antiquis dicta sunt,aggredi,ab altioribus quidem quæstionibus absti-nensysimpticiores vero mediocriter conjectans.
passages.english: Since, Chrysaorius, it is necessary, both for the teaching on the categories found in Aristotle and for the assigning of definitions, and generally for the things that belong to division and demonstration, to know what genus is, what difference, what species, what property and what accident, and since the study of these things is useful, I shall give you a concise account. I shall try briefly, by way of an introduction, to approach what has been said by the ancients, abstaining from the deeper questions and treating the simpler ones in moderation.
passages.notes: Scan errors corrected: genu.s, el, utili itarum (utili istarum), tradilionem, absti-nensysimpticiores (abstinens, simpliciores). 'Conjectans' is read as 'conjectans' (treating, reasoning about); its exact sense here is uncertain.

passages.original: Eorum enim quas prædicantur, alia quidem de uno dicuntur solo, sicut individua, ut Socrates, et hic et hoc;alia vero de plurinus, quemadmodum genera et species, et differentia J et propria, et accidentia communiter, sed non proprie alicui. Est autem genus qui. dem,ut animal;species vero ut homo : differentia, ut - rationale;
passages.english: For of the things that are predicated, some are said of one alone, as individuals are, for example Socrates, and "this man" and "this thing"; others of several, as genera and species, and differences and properties, and accidents in a common way, but not properly of any one thing. A genus is, for example, animal; a species, for example, man; a difference, for example, rational;
passages.notes: "plurinus" read as "pluribus"; stray "J" after "differentia" omitted. "Accidents in a common way, but not properly of any one thing" renders "accidentia communiter, sed non proprie alicui"; the phrasing is compressed and the sense somewhat uncertain.

passages.original: Homo enim cum sit species, prædicatur de Socrate, Platone et caeteris quas a se non specie disjuncta sunt,sicuthomo atque equus vel bos, sed numero, quod quidem habet dubitationem quid sit hoc quod numero dicitur differre.Numeroenim differre aliquid videbitur quoties numerus a numero differt, ut grex boum qui fortassecontinet triginta boves differt n umero ah alio boum grege, si centum continet in se boves : in eo enim quod grex est, non differt, neque in eo quod boves, nec nisi numero quidem differunt, quod illi plures, illi vero sunt pauciores. Quomodo igitur Socrates et Plato specie non differunt, sed numero, cum et Socrates unus sit, et Plato unus, et unitas numero ab unitate non differat ? sed itaintelligendum est quod dictum est, numero differentibus, id eat in numerando differentibus, hoc est dum nume- rantur difFerentibus : cum enim dicimus hic Plato est, hic Socrates, duas fecimus unitates, ac si digito tangamus dicentes, hic unus est de Socrate, rursus de Platone hie unus est, non eadem unitas in Socrate numerata est quæ in Platone ;
passages.english: For man, since it is a species, is predicated of Socrates, Plato and the others, which are separated from one another not in species, as man and horse or ox are, but in number. This raises a difficulty: what is meant by saying that things differ in number? For something will seem to differ in number whenever a number differs from a number, as a herd of oxen which contains perhaps thirty oxen differs in number from another herd of oxen, if it contains a hundred oxen. For they do not differ in being a herd, nor in being oxen, and they differ only in number, in that the one is more and the other fewer. How then do Socrates and Plato differ not in species but in number, since Socrates is one and Plato is one, and a unit does not differ in number from a unit? But what was said, "differing in number", must be understood thus: differing in the numbering, that is, differing while they are being counted. For when we say "this is Plato, this is Socrates", we have made two units, just as if we touched [them] with a finger, saying of Socrates "this is one", and again of Plato "this is one"; the same unit has not been counted in Socrates as in Plato;

passages.original: Tria hæc esse diximus qure significationem hanc tertiam generis informarent, id est de pluribus praedicari,despeciedifferentibus, et in eo quod quid sit, quae singulæ partes genus a caeteris quæ quomodo- libet praedicantur distribuunt ac secernunt, quod ipse breviter colligens dicit: id enim quod de pluribus praedicatur genus ab his dividitquaedeuno tantum prædicantur individuo.Individuum autem pluribus dicitur modis : dicitur individuum quod omnino secari non potest, ut unitas vel mens ; dicitur individuum quod ob soliditatem dividi nequit, ut adamas ; dicitur individuum cujus prædicatio in reliqua similia non convenit,ut Socrates : nam cum illi sint cæteri homines similes, non convenit proprietas et praedicatio Socratis in caeteris ; ergo ab iis quai de uno tantum prædicantur genus differt, eo quod de pluribuspraedicetur.Restantigitur quatuor,species, et proprium, et differentia, et accidens, quorum a genere differentias colligamus, Singulis igitur differentiis ab his rebus segregabitur genus : ea quidem differentia quae de specie differentibus prædicari genus dicitur, separamur ab his quae sicut species prædicantur, vel sicut propria ;
passages.english: We said that there are these three things which shape this third meaning of genus, namely being predicated of several things, of things differing in species, and in respect of what it is; and these individual parts distinguish and separate genus from the other things which are predicated in any way whatever. Gathering this briefly, he himself says: for the fact that it is predicated of several things divides genus from those which are predicated of one individual only. "Individual" is said in several ways: that is called individual which cannot be cut at all, such as a unit or a mind; that is called individual which cannot be divided because of its solidity, such as adamant; that is called individual whose predication does not fit other similar things, such as Socrates: for although other men are similar to him, the property and predication of Socrates does not fit the others. Therefore genus differs from those things which are predicated of one only, in that it is predicated of several. There remain, then, four, species, property, difference and accident, and let us gather their differences from genus. By individual differences, then, genus will be set apart from these things: by the difference by which genus is said to be predicated of things differing in species, we separate [it] from those which are predicated as species, or as properties;
passages.notes: "adamas" (adamant) may mean diamond or a hard metal.

passages.original: Deum vero dico corporeum, hunc enim mundum veteres Deum vocabant,etJoviseum appellatione dignati sunt, Deumque, solem, caeteraque cælestia corpora, quae animata esse cum Plato, tum plurimus doctorum chorus arbitratus est, sub homine vero individui singularesque homines sunt, ut Plato, Cato, Cicero, quorum numerum pluralitas infinitanon recipit.,cujus rei subjecta descriptio sub oculis ponat exemplum.
passages.english: By 'God' I mean a corporeal [god]. For the ancients called this world God, and honoured it with the name of Jupiter. And [they called] God the sun and the other heavenly bodies, which Plato, and also a very large chorus of learned men, judged to be animate. Under man are the individual and singular men, such as Plato, Cato and Cicero, whose number an infinite plurality does not admit [of being counted]. Let the diagram below set an example of this before the eyes.
passages.notes: 'quorum numerum pluralitas infinita non recipit' is awkward Latin and the rendering is uncertain. The diagram referred to is not included.

passages.original: Reliquas enim partes rationale atque mortale adduntur animali ad diffiniendam substantiam hominis: homo vero Socratis atque Ciceronis tota substantia est: nulla enim additur differentia substantialis ad hominem, ut Socrates fiat aut Cicero, sicut additur animali rationale atque mortale, ut homo integra diffinitione claudatur. Idcirco igitur species specialissima tantum est species, atque hanc solam possidet habitudinem ad superiora quidem, quoniam ab his continetur: ad inferiora vero, quoniam substantiam eorum format et continet.
passages.english: For the remaining parts, rational and mortal, are added to animal to define the substance of man; but man is the whole substance of Socrates and of Cicero: for no substantial difference is added to man so that Socrates or Cicero may come to be, as rational and mortal are added to animal so that man may be enclosed by a complete definition. For this reason, then, the most specific species is only a species, and possesses this single relation: to the higher things, since it is contained by them; and to the lower, since it forms and contains their substance.

passages.original: In generibus autem et speciebus non sic se ltabet.Neque enim unum commune genus omnium est ens, nec omnia ejusdem generis suntsecundum unum supremum genus, quemadmodum dicit Aristoteles, sed sine posila, quemadmodum dictum est in prædicamentis.prima decem genera, quasi decem prima principia. Ei si omnia quis entia vocet,aequivocefinquit, nuncupabitnonunivoce : si enim ens unum esset commune omnium genus, univoce omnia entia dicerentur: cum vero sint decem prima, commune est ens secundum nomen solum, non etiam secundum rationem, quas secundum entis nomen est.
passages.english: With genera and species, however, it is not so. For being is not one common genus of all things, nor are all things of the same genus according to one supreme genus, as Aristotle says. Rather, as was said in the Categories, the ten first genera are posited as ten first principles. And if someone calls all things beings, he says, he will name them equivocally, not univocally. For if being were one common genus of all things, all things would be called beings univocally. But since there are ten first [genera], being is common in name only, not also in the account that corresponds to the name of being.
passages.notes: 'sine posila' read as 'sint posita'. 'quas' read as 'quae'.

passages.original: Si igitur quoniam esse de omnibus his prsedicatur,omnium genus erit ens:etunum, quoniam de omnibus praedicatur,erit omnium genus, sed unum atque ens (utdemonstratum est) minimealterum alteripraeponitur; duo igitur aequaliasingulorum praedicamentorum genera sunt, quod fieri nequit: cum boc igitur ita sit, id Porphyrius determinavit dicens ; non ita in rebus,ut in familiis omnia ad unum principium posse deduci, ne omnium rerum commune esse genus posse,ut Aristoteli placet,sedsunt praeposita, inquit,quemadmodum in prædicamentis dictum est, prima decem genera quasi decem prima principia, scilicet utjnullainlerim ratioperquiratur,sedArislotelis auctori tati concedentes,haec decem genera nulli alii generi credamus esse subjecta,quce si quis entia vocet aequivoce nuncupabit,non univoce,neque enim unaeorum omnium secundumcommunenomendiffinitio poteritadhiberi,quaeresfacit, ut non univoce de his aliquid praedicetur.
passages.english: If, then, because being is predicated of all these, being will be the genus of all, then 'one' too, because it is predicated of all, will be the genus of all. But one and being (as has been shown) are in no way placed one above the other. So there would be two equal genera of each of the categories, which cannot happen. Since this is so, Porphyry settled it, saying that in things it is not as in families, where everything can be traced back to one origin. Nor can there be a common genus of all things, as Aristotle holds. Rather, he says, the ten first genera are set first, as was said in the Categories, as ten first principles. That is, for the present no argument is to be sought, but, yielding to Aristotle's authority, we are to believe that these ten genera are subject to no other genus. If someone calls these beings, he will name them equivocally, not univocally. For no single definition of them all according to the common name can be applied, and this makes it the case that something is not predicated of them univocally.
passages.notes: 'ne omnium' read as 'nec'. 'utjnullainlerim' read as 'ut nulla interim'.

passages.original: Specierum vero genera, et ita dicendum sit, genus quidemspeciesdistribuuntjetspeciesabindividuisin multitudinem deducuntur:rursusautem genus qui- i dem multas species colllgit.Species autem singula- ' rem particularemque multitudinern ab singularitatis deducit unitatem,igitur plus genus adunativum est quam species. Species namque sola individua colligit. Genus vero tam species quam ipsarum Iquoque specierum individuas contrahit singularesque personas, aed in hoc convenienti utitur exemplo dicens, participatione speciei, id est hominis Cato, Plato, Cicero pluresque reliqui homines: unus,idestmillia hominum in eo quod sunt homines, unus homo est. At vero est unus homo, qui specialis est, si ad nominummultitudinemquisubipsosuntconsideretur, plures fiuntjitaet plures homines in speciali homine unus est.Et specialis,unus est in pluribus infinitus.
passages.english: Of the species [there are] genera, if one must speak so. The species divide up the genus, and the species are drawn out into multitude by the individuals. Again, the genus gathers many species together, while the species draws a singular and particular multitude to the unity of singularity. Therefore the genus is more unifying than the species. For the species gathers only individuals, but the genus draws together both the species and the individual and singular persons of those species. He uses a fitting example for this, saying that by participation in the species, that is, man, Cato, Plato, Cicero and the many other men are one. That is, thousands of men, insofar as they are men, are one man. But the one man, who is the specific [man], if he is considered with respect to the multitude of names under him, becomes many. So the many men are one in the specific man, and the specific [man], being one, is infinite in the many.
passages.notes: The opening clause is obscure; 'et ita' is perhaps for 'si ita'. 'ab singularitatis deducit unitatem' is garbled in syntax. 'aed' is read as 'sed'. 'nominum' may be an error for 'hominum'. The passage seems a loose paraphrase of Porphyry and its wording is uncertain in places.

passages.original: Ultimum vero genus id autem est quod ante specialissimas species collocatur sine medio,etde solis speciebus specialissimis dici potest et de earum individuis : species vero de individuis,ut dictum est,individua enim de singulis praedicantur, ut Socrates et Plato, eaque maxime sunt individua,quae sub ostensione, indicationeque digiti eadunt,ut hoc scamnum,et hie veniens,eaque quae ex aliqua proprietate accidentium designantur nota,ut si quis Socratem significatione velit ostendere, non dicat Socrates, ne sit alius qui forte hoc nomine nuncupetur,sed dicat Sophronisci filius,si unicus Sophronisci fuerit: individua enim maxime ostendi queunt,si vel tacito nomine,sensui ipsioculorum digito, tactuve monstrentur, vel ex aliquo proprio nomine,si solus illud adeptus est,nomen : vel si ex parentibus,si illorum est unicus filius, vel si ex quolibet alio accidenti singularitasdemonstratur,eo quod accidentia ad unam se praedicationem habeant,ejusque vel prædicatio vel dictio non trans- eat ad alterum,sicut genens quod ad species, specierum vero ad individua.
passages.english: The lowest genus is that which is placed immediately before the most specific species, and it can be predicated only of the most specific species and of their individuals; species, as has been said, [are predicated] of individuals; for individuals are predicated of single things, such as Socrates and Plato. Those are most of all individuals which fall under pointing and the indication of the finger, such as "this bench" and "this man coming," and those which are designated by a mark from some property of accidents: for example, if someone wished to point out Socrates by signification, he would not say "Socrates," lest there be someone else perhaps called by this name, but would say "the son of Sophroniscus," if he were Sophroniscus' only son. For individuals can best be pointed out if, with the name left unspoken, they are shown to the very sense of the eyes by the finger or by touch; or by some proper name, if he alone has obtained that name; or from the parents, if he is their only son; or if the singularity is shown from any other accident, because the accidents relate to a single predication, and its predication or expression does not pass over to another, as that of the genus does to the species, and that of the species to the individuals.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected ("eadunt" = cadunt, "hie" = hic, "genens" = generis/genus). The final clause is somewhat compressed in the Latin.

passages.original: Distat item inseparabilibus accidentibus, quod hic ' statutæ sit longioris,hic minime.Quæ cum itasint,in ternariumnumerumhasdifferentiarum diversitates Porphyrius colligit, hisque ipse nomina quibus post utatur,apponit,dicens : Omnis. differentia vel communiter vel propria,vel magis propria nuncupatur. Communiter quidem eam differentiam sumens quae quodlibet accidens monstraret,quæ in quadam alteritate consistit, ut si Plato a Socrate differat quod ille sedeat,hic ambulet,vel quod ille senex, hic vero sit juvenis;a seipso etiam saepe aliquis differre potest; ut si nunc quidem faciat aliquid cum ante quieverit, vel si nunc adolescens jam faotus si t,cumprius te- nera vixisset infantia.CommuneB autem differentiae nuncupatae sunt,quoniam nullius propriae esse possunt differentiæ,et quae separabilia accidentia sola significant.Nam et stare et sedere et facere aliquid ac non facere,multorum atque adeo omnium sunt, et separabiliaesseaccidentiamanifestumest.Quibus si qua differunt,communibus differentiis distare dicuntur.Praeterea puerum esse atque adolescentem vel senem,ea quoque veraciter separabilia sunt accidentia.Nam ex pueritia ad adolescentiam,atque hinc ad senectutem,ab hac denique ad decrepitam usque aetatem ,naturae ipsius necessitate progredimur.Illud forsitansitdubitabiledeuniuscujusque formacorporis,an ullo modo separari queat.Sed ea quoque est separabilis forma,nullius enim diuturna ac stabilis formaperdurat.ldcirconec peregrinus pater relictum domi puerum,si adolescentem redux viderit,potest agnoscere:forma enim semper quae antefuerat,permutatur,atque ipsa alteritas qua distamus ab altera semper diversa est.Constat igitur;hanc communem differentiam separabilibus maxime accidentibus applicari,propria vero est quæ inseparabilia significat accidentia.Ea hujusmodi sunt ut si quis caesiis nascatur oculis, si qui incurvo naso:dumenim adest nasus atque oculi, ille ceesius, ille semper erit incurvus,atque hoc per naturam.
passages.english: He likewise differs by inseparable accidents, in that this one is of taller stature, that one not. Since this is so, Porphyry gathers these varieties of differences into a threefold number, and himself assigns them names that he may use afterwards, saying: "Every difference is called either common, or proper, or most proper." He takes as common that difference which would show any accident whatever, which consists in a certain otherness: as if Plato differs from Socrates in that the one sits and the other walks, or in that the one is old and the other young; and someone can often differ even from himself, as if he now does something when before he was at rest, or if he has now become a youth when previously he lived in tender infancy. They are called common differences because they can be proper to no one, and they signify separable accidents only. For standing and sitting and doing something and not doing it belong to many, indeed to all, and it is clear that they are separable accidents. If any things differ by these, they are said to differ by common differences. Moreover, being a boy or a youth or an old man, these too are truly separable accidents. For from boyhood to youth, and from there to old age, and from this finally to decrepit age, we advance by the necessity of nature itself. It might perhaps be doubted concerning the bodily form of each person whether it can in any way be separated. But that form too is separable, for no one's form endures long and stable. Therefore a father who has travelled abroad, if on his return he sees as a youth the boy he left at home, cannot recognise him: for the form that existed before is always being changed, and the very otherness by which we differ from another is always different. It is established, then, that this common difference applies chiefly to separable accidents, while proper [difference] is that which signifies inseparable accidents. These are of this kind: if someone is born with grey-blue eyes, or someone with a hooked nose; for while the nose and eyes remain, the one will always be grey-eyed, the other always hook-nosed, and this by nature.
passages.notes: "nec" (idcirco nec ... potest) taken as negating "potest agnoscere".

passages.original: Deus autem cum sit animal, ut de sole dicamus, rationali immortalique efficitur differentiis, quas dividere genus habita partitio paulo monstravit. Sed hic (ut di- aimus) Deum corporeum intelligi oportl't,ut solem et cælum caeteraque hujusmodi,quæ cum animata et rationabilia Plato esse confirmat,tum in deorum vo- cabulum antiquitatis veneratione probantur assum- pIa, de primo quoque genere, id est substantia do- monstrantur venire differentiæ.Nam cum ej us divisivae sint differentiae animatum atque inanimatum, sensibile atque insensibile,juncta' differentiae sensibilis atque animatiefficiuntsubstantiam animatam atque sensibilem, quod est animal.
passages.english: God, since he is an animal (let us speak of the sun), is produced by the differences rational and immortal, which the division given a little earlier showed to divide the genus. But here (as we said) God must be understood as corporeal, like the sun, the heavens and other such things. Plato affirms that these are animate and rational, and they are also shown to have been taken up into the name of gods by the veneration of antiquity. The differences are also shown to come from the first genus, that is, substance. For since its dividing differences are animate and inanimate, sensible and insensible, the differences sensible and animate, when joined, produce animate and sensible substance, which is animal.
passages.notes: Scan errors corrected: di-aimus, oportl't, assum-pIa, do-monstrantur, ej us.

passages.original: Species vero de suis tantum individuis praedicatur : neque enim fieri potest, ut quae species est ultima quaeque vere species ac magis species nuncupatur, hæc alias deducatur in species ; quod si ita est, sola post speciem individua restant : jure igitur species de suistantum individuis prædicatur,ut homode Socrate, Platone, Cicerone, et cæteris. Proprium item de specie prædicaturcujus est proprium,nequeenim esset proprium alicujus ei de aliquo prædicaretur, de quo enim quæque res, etsoli etomni, et semper dicitur, ejusdem proprium esse monstratur: quæ cum ita sint, proprium de specie dicitur, ut risibile de homine, omnis enim homo risibilis est.
passages.english: A species, however, is predicated only of its own individuals: for it cannot happen that what is the lowest species, and is called truly and most properly a species, should be brought down into other species; and if this is so, after the species only individuals remain. Rightly, then, a species is predicated only of its own individuals, as man of Socrates, Plato, Cicero and the rest. Likewise a property is predicated of the species of which it is the property; for it would not be the property of something if it were predicated of something [else], for that of which each thing is said, both alone and of all and always, is shown to be that whose property it is. Since this is so, a property is said of a species, as risible of man, for every man is risible.
passages.notes: "ei de aliquo" read as "si de alio" or similar; sense uncertain.

passages.original: Sed multo magis separabilia accidentia pluribus inhærescunt, ut moveri homini, et bovi; uterque enim movetur.Et rursus ea quæ sub homine sunt atque bove individua, moveri sæpe prædicantur. Sed advertendum est, auctore Porphyrio, quod ea quae accidentia sunt principaliter quidem de his dicuntur,in quibussuntindividuis :secundoveroloco, ad universalia individuorum referuntur, atque ita praedicatio subteriorum superioribus redditur, ut quoniam nigredo singulis corvis adesse dicitur,dicitur etiam adesse speciali corvo.
passages.english: But separable accidents inhere in many things much more, as being moved [belongs] to a man and to an ox, for both are moved. And again, the individuals that fall under man and ox are often said to be moved. But it must be noted, on Porphyry's authority, that accidents are said principally of the individuals in which they are, and in the second place are referred to the universals of the individuals. Thus the predication of the lower things is rendered to the higher: since blackness is said to be present in individual crows, it is said also to be present in the specific crow.

passages.original: genera uero et species naturaliter priora sunt individuis substantiis.Et genera quidem in eo quod quid sit prædicantur de his quæ sub ipsis sunt : accidenUa vero in eo quod quale aliquid sit, tIel quomodo se habet unumquodque : qualis est enim Æthiops interrogatus, dicis,niger; et quomodo Socrates se habet, dicis, sedet vel ambulat.
passages.english: but genera and species are by nature prior to individual substances. And genera are predicated, in respect of what it is, of the things under them; but accidents in respect of what sort something is, or how each thing is disposed: for asked what sort an Ethiopian is, you say "black"; and [asked] how Socrates is disposed, you say "he is sitting" or "walking".

passages.original: id quoque commune est speciei cum genere,genus quippe ab accidenti in eo quod quid est,et quomodo se habeat praedicatione dividitur. Item unamquamque substantiam una videtur species continere,ut Socratem homo,atque ideo Socrati una tantum propinquitas speciei est hominis.Rursus individuo equo una species equiest proxima,itemque in caeteris:unicuiqueenim substantiae una species praeest, at vero unicuique substantias non unum accidens jungitur:unicuique enim substantiae plura semper accidentia supervenunt, ut Socrati quod calvus, quod simus, quod glaucus, quod propenso ventre, et in aliis quidem aubstantiis de numero accidentium idem convenit dicere.
passages.english: this too the species has in common with the genus, for genus is divided from accident by predication, the one in respect of what a thing is, the other of how it is disposed. Again, one species seems to contain each substance, as man [contains] Socrates, and therefore Socrates has a nearness to only one species, that of man. Again, to the individual horse one species, that of horse, is nearest, and likewise in the rest: for one species presides over each substance, but not one accident is joined to each substance: for several accidents always come upon each substance, as to Socrates that he is bald, snub-nosed, grey-eyed, pot-bellied; and in other substances too it is fitting to say the same about the number of accidents.
passages.notes: The first sentence is compressed; it seems to mean that genus, like species, is distinguished from accident by being predicated 'what it is' rather than 'how it is disposed'.
